stem:
On day 5 after an admission for pneumonia, a 70-kg 78-year-old is eating meals and drinking about 1.8 L a day without vomiting, diarrhoea or other abnormal losses. Maintenance IV fluid has run at 100 mL/h since admission. Today he has new ankle oedema and fine bibasal crackles, his weight is 3 kg above admission, and sodium is 133 mmol/L (135–145). Blood pressure and urine output are normal.

What is the most appropriate fluid plan?

options.label: A
options.text: Continue the IV fluid at the same rate and add furosemide
options.explanation: Giving a diuretic to remove fluid that is still being infused unnecessarily treats the result rather than the cause.

options.label: B
options.text: Halve the IV rate and recheck electrolytes in 24 hours
options.explanation: His oral intake already meets his needs, so any maintenance infusion is surplus while he is overloaded.

options.label: C
options.text: Stop the IV fluid; monitor intake, weight and electrolytes
options.explanation: Daily maintenance needs are roughly 25–30 mL/kg, about 1.75–2.1 L for him, which his oral intake now meets. The 2.4 L of IV fluid a day is surplus, causing overload and dilutional hyponatraemia. Maintenance IV fluid is indicated only when oral intake cannot meet needs, so it is stopped.

options.label: D
options.text: Change the infusion to 0.9% saline to correct the sodium
options.explanation: The low sodium is dilutional from excess fluid; more fluid of any kind adds to the overload.

options.label: E
options.text: Continue the IV fluid and restrict oral fluid to 1 L a day
options.explanation: Restricting normal drinking to keep a drip running reverses the right priority; oral intake should replace IV fluid.

context: Maintenance IV fluid is only for patients whose oral or enteral intake cannot meet daily needs (about 25–30 mL/kg); once intake is adequate, stop it, especially if overload appears.
